concept.name: Law of supply and demand
concept.definition: Wyckoff's first law: when demand exceeds supply, prices rise; when supply exceeds demand, prices fall; and the balance is judged by comparing price and volume bars on a chart. It is the foundational heuristic of the method, a framework for reading charts rather than a measurable law of nature.
concept.intuition: More buyers than sellers pushes price up, more sellers than buyers pushes it down — and the tape tells you which side is winning.
concept.mechanics: The analyst compares consecutive bars' spread, close location, and volume: wide-spread bars closing near highs on rising volume indicate demand, while wide-spread bars closing near lows on rising volume indicate supply. This bar-by-bar reading underlies the labeling of all Wyckoff events and phases.
concept.failure_modes: The principle is tautological at the margin — price always moves to equilibrate orders — and reading which side is 'really' in control from bar data is subjective and error-prone, especially in news-driven or illiquid markets.
concept.misconceptions: It is called a law but is an analytical guideline; volume and spread do not reveal institutional intent mechanically, and accurate supply/demand reading takes substantial practice, as Wyckoff teaching itself concedes.
concept.example: During a pullback, each successive down-bar has narrower spread and lower volume, while the following rally expands in both; the analyst concludes demand dominates supply and the uptrend should resume.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
citations.section: The Basic Principles: Three Wyckoff Laws (Law 1); Supply and Demand Analysis
